solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know that Tibetan refugees occupy a special status in India and that India has not deported them may think they have some form of citizenship or quasi-citizenship, making them appear similar to the other options.
elimination_logic: Identify the common category among three options — statuses that involve some degree of quasi-citizenship or formal legal arrangement conferring Indian rights.
OCI status: provides lifelong visa and certain rights — formally defined in law.
Naturalized citizenship: full Indian citizenship after renouncing foreign nationality — clearly in the category.
PIO card (pre-2015): gave certain privileges to persons of Indian origin — a formal status now merged with OCI.

Tibetan refugee status: is not a defined citizenship-adjacent status in Indian law — Tibetans in India are registered foreigners under the Foreigners Act, without any formal citizenship-related rights framework, making this the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap here merges the informal political accommodation of Tibetan refugees (permitted to reside, operate schools, have a government-in-exile) with a formal legal status akin to OCI or PIO. In law, Tibetan refugees are registered foreigners under the Foreigners Registration Act — they hold no Indian citizenship, no OCI status, and no PIO privileges. Their continued presence is governed by administrative tolerance, not by any citizenship-related statute. Students who focus on India's sympathetic posture toward Tibet may conflate political accommodation with legal citizenship-adjacent status.
solution.final_explanation:
India's citizenship framework creates formal statuses — citizenship, OCI, and (formerly) PIO cards — with statutory definitions and legally defined rights and restrictions.

• Option (a) — OCI status: Formally defined under the Citizenship Act 1955 (Section 7A onwards). OCI holders receive lifelong multi-entry visas and specific economic rights. It is a citizenship-adjacent status in Indian law.
• Option (b) — Tibetan refugee status: Tibetans in India are registered under the Foreigners Registration Act as foreign nationals. They hold no OCI, no PIO privileges, and no citizenship-related statutory status. Their presence is administratively tolerated, not legally formalised as citizenship-adjacent. This is the odd one out.
• Option (c) — Naturalized Indian citizenship: Full Indian citizenship acquired under Section 6 — the most complete status possible.
• Option (d) — PIO card (pre-2015): Was a formally defined status under the Citizenship Act giving PIOs certain rights — now merged into OCI but was a legally recognised status.

Value Addition:
• Tibetan children born in India before 1987 can claim Indian citizenship by birth under the pre-1987 unconditional jus soli rule.
• The Foreigners Act 1946 and Foreigners Registration Order 1939 govern the registration of foreigners including refugees in India.
• India has not signed the 1951 UN Refugee Convention — refugee status in India is entirely a matter of administrative policy, not statutory right.

elimination_logic: तीन विकल्पों में सामान्य श्रेणी की पहचान करें — वे दर्जे जो कुछ हद तक अर्ध-नागरिकता या भारतीय अधिकार प्रदान करने वाले औपचारिक कानूनी व्यवस्था से संबंधित हैं।
OCI स्थिति: आजीवन वीज़ा और कुछ अधिकार प्रदान करती है — विधिवत कानून में परिभाषित।
प्राकृतिककरण द्वारा नागरिकता: विदेशी नागरिकता त्यागने के बाद पूर्ण भारतीय नागरिकता — स्पष्ट रूप से इसी श्रेणी में।
PIO कार्ड (2015 से पहले): भारतीय मूल के व्यक्तियों को कुछ विशेषाधिकार देता था — एक औपचारिक दर्जा जो अब OCI में विलयित है।

तिब्बती शरणार्थी स्थिति: भारतीय कानून में कोई परिभाषित नागरिकता-संबंधित दर्जा नहीं है — भारत में तिब्बती विदेशी अधिनियम के तहत पंजीकृत विदेशी हैं, जिनके पास कोई औपचारिक नागरिकता-संबंधित अधिकार नहीं है, इसलिए यह अलग विकल्प है।
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: यह भ्रम का जाल तिब्बती शरणार्थियों के अनौपचारिक राजनीतिक आवास (जो निवास करने, स्कूल चलाने, निर्वासित सरकार रखने की अनुमति रखते हैं) को OCI या PIO जैसे औपचारिक कानूनी दर्जे के साथ मिला देता है। कानून में, तिब्बती शरणार्थी विदेशी पंजीकरण अधिनियम के तहत पंजीकृत विदेशी हैं — उनके पास न तो भारतीय नागरिकता है, न OCI स्थिति, न PIO विशेषाधिकार। उनकी उपस्थिति प्रशासनिक सहिष्णुता पर आधारित है, न कि किसी नागरिकता-संबंधित कानून पर। जो छात्र भारत की तिब्बत के प्रति सहानुभूतिपूर्ण नीति पर ध्यान केंद्रित करते हैं, वे राजनीतिक आवास को कानूनी नागरिकता-संबंधित दर्जे के साथ भ्रमित कर सकते हैं।
solution.final_explanation:
भारत की नागरिकता संरचना औपचारिक दर्जे बनाती है — नागरिकता, OCI, और (पूर्व में) PIO कार्ड — जिनकी वैधानिक परिभाषाएँ और कानूनी अधिकार एवं प्रतिबंध होते हैं।

• विकल्प (a) — OCI स्थिति: नागरिकता अधिनियम 1955 (धारा 7A से आगे) के तहत विधिवत परिभाषित। OCI धारकों को आजीवन बहु-प्रवेश वीज़ा और विशिष्ट आर्थिक अधिकार मिलते हैं। यह भारतीय कानून में नागरिकता-संबंधित दर्जा है।
• विकल्प (b) — तिब्बती शरणार्थी स्थिति: भारत में तिब्बती विदेशी पंजीकरण अधिनियम के तहत विदेशी नागरिक के रूप में पंजीकृत हैं। उनके पास न OCI है, न PIO विशेषाधिकार, और न ही कोई नागरिकता-संबंधित वैधानिक दर्जा। उनकी उपस्थिति प्रशासनिक सहिष्णुता पर आधारित है, न कि कानूनी रूप से नागरिकता-संबंधित। यह अलग विकल्प है।
• विकल्प (c) — प्राकृतिककरण द्वारा भारतीय नागरिकता: धारा 6 के तहत प्राप्त पूर्ण भारतीय नागरिकता — सबसे पूर्ण दर्जा।
• विकल्प (d) — PIO कार्ड (2015 से पहले): नागरिकता अधिनियम के तहत विधिवत परिभाषित दर्जा था जो PIO को कुछ अधिकार देता था — अब OCI में विलयित, लेकिन कानूनी रूप से मान्यता प्राप्त दर्जा था।

मूल्यवर्धन:
• 1987 से पहले भारत में जन्मे तिब्बती बच्चे बिना शर्त जन्मसिद्ध अधिकार (jus soli) के तहत भारतीय नागरिकता का दावा कर सकते हैं।
• विदेशी अधिनियम 1946 और विदेशी पंजीकरण आदेश 1939 भारत में शरणार्थियों सहित विदेशी नागरिकों के पंजीकरण को नियंत्रित करते हैं।
• भारत ने 1951 के UN शरणार्थी सम्मेलन पर हस्ताक्षर नहीं किए हैं — भारत में शरणार्थी स्थिति पूरी तरह प्रशासनिक नीति का विषय है, न कि वैधानिक अधिकार।

statement_analysis.statement: The Citizenship Amendment Act 2019 extends the reduced naturalization pathway to members of the Ahmadiyya community from Pakistan.
statement_analysis.reason: The Ahmadiyya community is a Muslim sect — and Muslims are explicitly not included among the six beneficiary communities listed in the CAA 2019. The Act covers Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian communities only.

statement_analysis.statement: Sri Lanka is one of the three countries from which applicants may claim the benefit of the CAA 2019 reduced naturalization pathway.
statement_analysis.reason: The three countries specified in the CAA 2019 are Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan — Sri Lanka is not included, despite hosting significant Tamil Hindu refugee populations.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the CAA 2019, a Buddhist from Myanmar who entered India after December 2014 is eligible for the reduced 5-year naturalization pathway.
statement_analysis.reason: Myanmar is not one of the three specified countries under the CAA 2019 (Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan); and the cut-off date is entry on or before 31st December 2014, not after.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly identify Ahmadiyyas as a Muslim sect (excluded) but incorrectly include Sri Lanka as a specified country may select option (a) thinking only Statement 1 is incorrect.
elimination_logic: Reject Statement 1 as correct — Ahmadiyyas are Muslim, and Muslims are not a beneficiary community under CAA 2019.
Reject Statement 2 as correct — the three specified countries are Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan; Sri Lanka is conspicuously absent despite Tamil refugee issues.
Reject Statement 3 as correct — Myanmar is not specified, and entry must be on or before 31st December 2014, not after.
All three statements are incorrect — the answer is option (c), asking which are NOT correct, which is all three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's entity-swap exploits the fact that Sri Lanka's Tamil Hindu refugees are a politically prominent group and students may assume CAA 2019 covers them. The Act's three specified countries — Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan — are all Muslim-majority countries that are India's neighbours, and the legislative intent was specifically about partition-related or Islamic-state-related persecution. Sri Lanka's Tamil issues are ethnicity-based, not religion-based persecution in the same mould, and the country was deliberately excluded.
solution.final_explanation:
The CAA 2019 is precisely worded and limited in its scope. Misidentifying the covered communities, countries, or cut-off date is a common examination error.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Ahmadiyyas, despite facing severe persecution in Pakistan, are classified as a Muslim sect under Pakistani law. The CAA's beneficiary list covers only Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian — explicitly excluding Muslims.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The three specified source countries are Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan. Sri Lanka is not included. Tamil Hindus and Tamil Christians from Sri Lanka cannot claim CAA 2019 benefits.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Two errors: Myanmar is not a specified country, and the cut-off is entry on or BEFORE 31st December 2014, not after. A post-2014 entrant from a specified country is also excluded.

Value Addition:
• The Ahmadiyya exclusion is particularly controversial because they face state-sponsored persecution under Pakistan's blasphemy laws.
• The omission of Sri Lanka has been noted as a gap — Tamil refugees fleeing the civil war include both Hindus and Christians who could have been included.
• The cut-off date of 31st December 2014 predates the Act's passage by five years — it is a retrospective eligibility condition.

elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The First Schedule to the Citizenship Act 1955 prescribes the form of the oath of allegiance, which requires the person to renounce all other allegiances and bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. India prohibits dual citizenship under the Citizenship Act 1955 — a person who acquires Indian citizenship must not simultaneously hold citizenship of another country.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. The oath's requirement of renouncing prior nationality is directly caused by India's prohibition on dual citizenship. If India permitted dual citizenship, there would be no need to include renunciation in the oath.
Both A and R are correct and R explains A — the answer is (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The oath of allegiance prescribed in the First Schedule is not merely a ceremonial formality — it has substantive legal content. Two elements are central: bearing true faith and allegiance to the Constitution, and renouncing all other allegiances (including prior citizenship).

• Assertion (A): Correct. The First Schedule oath requires the naturalization applicant to formally renounce every other citizenship or allegiance before receiving the certificate. This is a legally operative act — upon taking the oath, the prior citizenship is treated as renounced.
• Reason (R): Correct. India's Citizenship Act 1955 prohibits dual citizenship. A person who voluntarily acquires foreign citizenship loses Indian citizenship automatically under Section 9 — the same logic applies in reverse to naturalization.
• Causal link: Present and direct. R explains A. The oath mandates renunciation precisely because Indian law does not permit holding two citizenships simultaneously. The renunciation element in the oath implements the anti-dual-citizenship policy.

Value Addition:
• A false renunciation — taking the oath while secretly retaining foreign citizenship — is a ground for cancellation under Section 10's false representation clause.
• Some countries (e.g., USA, UK) permit their citizens to acquire other nationalities — when an Indian becomes a US citizen, Indian citizenship is automatically lost under Section 9.
• The oath's requirement of 'true faith and allegiance to the Constitution' mirrors the oath taken by public office holders under the Third Schedule to the Constitution.

मूल्यवर्धन:

• विकल्प (a) — गलत: पूरे देश में कोई NRC पूरा नहीं हुआ है। यह अभ्यास केंद्र सरकार द्वारा प्रस्तावित है लेकिन अब तक राष्ट्रीय स्तर पर लागू नहीं किया गया है।
• विकल्प (b) — सही: असम एकमात्र राज्य है जहाँ NRC अपडेट पूरा हुआ है। अंतिम सूची अगस्त 2019 में प्रकाशित हुई, जिसमें लगभग 1.9 मिलियन लोगों को शामिल नहीं किया गया जिनकी नागरिकता सत्यापित नहीं हो सकी।
• विकल्प (c) — गलत: पश्चिम बंगाल ने NRC का विरोध राजनीतिक रूप से किया है लेकिन कोई NRC प्रक्रिया पूरी नहीं की है।
• विकल्प (d) — गलत: त्रिपुरा में प्रवासन संबंधी चिंताएं हैं लेकिन कोई NRC प्रक्रिया पूरी नहीं हुई है।

मूल्य संवर्धन:
• असम NRC की कट-ऑफ तिथि 24 मार्च 1971 बांग्लादेश मुक्ति युद्ध की शुरुआत से मेल खाती है — एक महत्वपूर्ण ऐतिहासिक आधार।
• असम NRC से बाहर किए गए लोगों को विदेशी न्यायाधिकरणों के समक्ष अपील करने का अधिकार है — उन्हें तुरंत विदेशी घोषित नहीं किया जाता।
• NRC और प्राकृतिककरण के बीच संबंध अप्रत्यक्ष है — NRC से बाहर किए गए व्यक्तियों को कानूनी प्रक्रिया के माध्यम से अपनी नागरिकता स्थापित करनी होती है, न कि प्राकृतिककरण के लिए आवेदन करके।

Section 6 of the Citizenship Act 1955 contains both the standard naturalization pathway and a special waiver provision. Section 6(2) allows the Central Government to relax or waive the Third Schedule qualifications entirely for persons who have rendered distinguished service to science, philosophy, art, literature, world peace, or human progress.

Akira: Japanese national, Nobel Prize in Chemistry, resident in India for 3 months — falling short of the 12-month continuous residence requirement. His contribution to science is unambiguously 'distinguished service to science' within Section 6(2).

• Option (b) — Incorrect: CAA 2019 applies only to six specified religious minorities from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan. Akira is a Japanese national — entirely outside this framework.

• Option (d) — Incorrect as stated: While government discretion exists broadly, it is Section 6(2) that specifically enables the waiver for Akira's category, making option (c) the more legally precise answer.

solution.final_explanation:
नागरिकता अधिनियम 1955 की धारा 6 में मानक naturalization मार्ग और एक विशेष छूट प्रावधान दोनों शामिल हैं। धारा 6(2) केंद्र सरकार को उन व्यक्तियों के लिए तीसरे अनुसूची की योग्यताओं को पूरी तरह या आंशिक रूप से छूट देने की अनुमति देती है जिन्होंने विज्ञान, दर्शन, कला, साहित्य, विश्व शांति, या मानव प्रगति में विशिष्ट सेवा दी हो।

अकिरा: जापानी नागरिक, रसायन विज्ञान में नोबेल पुरस्कार विजेता, भारत में 3 महीने का आवास — 12 महीने के निरंतर आवास की आवश्यकता पूरी नहीं करता। उनका विज्ञान में योगदान स्पष्ट रूप से धारा 6(2) के अंतर्गत 'विशिष्ट सेवा' है।

• विकल्प (a) — गलत: मानक तीसरे अनुसूची मार्ग में 12 महीने का निरंतर आवास आवश्यक है; अकिरा के 3 महीने इस आवश्यकता को पूरा नहीं करते, और मानक मार्ग में कोई छूट उपलब्ध नहीं है।
• विकल्प (b) — गलत: CAA 2019 केवल पाकिस्तान, बांग्लादेश, और अफगानिस्तान के छह निर्दिष्ट धार्मिक अल्पसंख्यकों पर लागू होता है। अकिरा जापानी नागरिक है — पूरी तरह से इस ढांचे के बाहर।
• विकल्प (c) — सही: धारा 6(2) अकिरा की स्थिति के लिए सटीक सक्षम प्रावधान है — यह विशिष्ट वैज्ञानिक उपलब्धि वाले व्यक्तियों के लिए आवास आवश्यकताओं को छूट देने की अनुमति देता है।
• विकल्प (d) — जैसा कि कहा गया है गलत: जबकि सरकार के पास व्यापक विवेकाधिकार है, विशिष्ट छूट धारा 6(2) के अंतर्गत आती है, जो अकिरा की श्रेणी के लिए छूट सक्षम करती है, इसलिए विकल्प (c) अधिक कानूनी रूप से सटीक उत्तर है।

मूल्य संवर्धन:
• धारा 6(2) का उपयोग दुर्लभ रूप से हुआ है — यह एक शक्तिशाली लेकिन कम उपयोग किया गया प्रावधान है।
• धारा 6(2) में 'विश्व शांति या मानव प्रगति' शब्द नोबेल शांति पुरस्कार विजेताओं, मानवीय कार्यकर्ताओं, और वैश्विक स्वास्थ्य चैंपियनों को भी कवर करने के लिए पर्याप्त व्यापक है।
• धारा 6(2) के बावजूद, सरकार के पास अंतिम विवेकाधिकार बना रहता है — यह प्रावधान naturalization देने के लिए बाध्य नहीं करता, केवल सक्षम करता है।

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know the 2005 OCI amendment and the 2003 Eighth Schedule amendment may reverse their order, placing the Eighth Schedule amendment after OCI introduction.
elimination_logic: Anchor Event 1: The Citizenship Act 1955 was enacted in 1955, the base legislation — this must come first.

solution.final_explanation:
Several significant amendments have shaped India's citizenship framework. Their chronological sequence reflects evolving policy priorities.

Correct sequence: 1955 → 2003 → 2005 → 2019

• 1955: Citizenship Act enacted — the foundational statutory framework for citizenship including naturalization.
• 2003: 92nd Constitutional Amendment added four languages to the Eighth Schedule — relevant to the naturalization language proficiency requirement.
• 2005: OCI status introduced through Citizenship (Amendment) Act — creating the citizenship-adjacent status for diaspora.
• 2019: CAA 2019 passed — reducing residence requirement for specified religious minorities from three countries.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Places 2005 OCI before 2003 Eighth Schedule amendment — reverses the correct order.
• Option (b) — Correct: 1955 → 2003 → 2005 → 2019 is the accurate chronological sequence.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Places CAA 2019 before the OCI introduction, which is impossible.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Begins with 2003, omitting the foundational 1955 Act's primacy.

Value Addition:
• The PIO card scheme (1999) predated OCI (2005) but was eventually absorbed into OCI in 2015.
• The Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2003 made significant changes to Section 3 (birth) by introducing conditional jus soli replacing the earlier unconditional approach.
• Understanding the amendment timeline helps distinguish the CAA 2019's novelty from earlier incremental changes.

solution.concept_anchor: Good character — subjective assessment and judicial review limits

statement_analysis.statement: The 'good character' requirement for naturalization under the Third Schedule is assessed subjectively by government authorities, without any statutory definition or exhaustive criteria prescribed in the Citizenship Act 1955.
statement_analysis.reason: The Citizenship Act deliberately leaves 'good character' undefined — it is evaluated on a case-by-case basis through police verification and security clearance, giving authorities wide discretion.

statement_analysis.statement: A court cannot examine the government's assessment of an applicant's 'good character' for any reason, as this assessment is entirely beyond judicial scrutiny.
statement_analysis.reason: While judicial review of naturalization decisions is limited, it is not completely excluded — courts can intervene in cases of mala fide exercise of power or procedural irregularity. 'Entirely beyond judicial scrutiny' is an over-extension.

solution.strong_distractor: a — The correct answer is actually (a), but students who know both statements relate to the broad discretionary-limited review principle may affirm both without catching the 'entirely beyond judicial scrutiny' absolute qualifier in Statement 2.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — 'good character' has no statutory definition; assessment is subjective and discretionary — this is settled law.
Test the absolute qualifier in Statement 2 — 'entirely beyond judicial scrutiny' is false; courts retain limited review for mala fides and procedural violations.
Since Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is incorrect, the answer is option (a) — Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap is embedded in Statement 2's absolute qualifier: 'entirely beyond judicial scrutiny.' Students who know the judicial review is 'highly limited' or 'restricted' may hastily read 'entirely beyond' as approximately correct. But the legal position is nuanced — limited is not zero. Courts have consistently maintained residual jurisdiction to review for mala fides. The word 'entirely' converts a true statement about restricted review into a false statement about zero review.
solution.final_explanation:
The 'good character' condition in the Third Schedule and the broader judicial review question both test the student's precision in reading legal propositions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: 'Good character' is an inherently subjective standard in the Citizenship Act. No statutory definition exists. Government authorities assess it through criminal records, intelligence reports, and police verification — a flexible, case-sensitive exercise of discretion.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The phrase 'entirely beyond judicial scrutiny' overstates the government's immunity. The Izhar Ahmad Khan case and subsequent decisions confirm that courts retain jurisdiction to examine naturalization decisions for mala fide intent and procedural irregularity. This is limited review, not zero review. The absolute qualifier makes Statement 2 false.

Value Addition:
• The mala fide standard for intervention means the court looks for evidence of personal bias or corrupt motivation — a very high bar to meet.
• Even for 'good character' assessments, if the government relies on a demonstrably false or fabricated adverse report, a court may intervene.
• The subjectivity of 'good character' is not unique to Indian law — most common law countries similarly treat character assessment as an executive prerogative in naturalization.

statement_analysis.statement: The principle of 'effective nationality' in international law is used to determine which country's citizenship claim prevails when a person holds dual citizenship and two states assert jurisdiction over them simultaneously.
statement_analysis.reason: Effective nationality (affirmed in the Nottebohm case by the ICJ) determines which nationality is 'genuine and effective' based on the person's habitual residence, centre of interests, and family ties — the stronger connection prevails.

statement_analysis.statement: India has ratified the 1961 United Nations Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness, which obligates state parties to grant citizenship to stateless persons born on their territory.
statement_analysis.reason: India has not ratified the 1961 UN Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness. India is not a party to this convention, though it has addressed statelessness to some extent through its domestic citizenship provisions.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Indian law, a person who is required by the law of their original country to renounce nationality but is unable to do so because that country does not permit formal renunciation is not automatically disqualified from naturalization.
statement_analysis.reason: The Citizenship Act 1955 contains an exception for cases where the law of the applicant's country does not permit renunciation — the government may proceed with naturalization despite this constraint.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who believe India, as a large democracy, must have ratified major UN conventions may affirm Statement 2 without independently verifying India's ratification status.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — the effective nationality doctrine from Nottebohm (1955) is a settled ICJ principle; it applies in dual citizenship disputes.

Reject Statement 2 — India has not ratified the 1961 Statelessness Convention; this is a factual position that students frequently get wrong by assuming India's ratification of other human rights instruments.
Confirm Statement 3 — the exception for countries not permitting renunciation is a pragmatic legislative provision preventing statelessness as an inadvertent outcome of naturalization requirements.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's partial-truth trap works because students know India has participated in international forums on statelessness and has signed various UN human rights conventions. The assumption is that India must have ratified the 1961 Convention since it deals with a humanitarian issue. But ratification and participation are different — India has chosen not to ratify several international conventions despite engaging with their subject matter domestically.
solution.final_explanation:
International law dimensions of naturalization involve statelessness prevention, the effective nationality principle, and the question of India's treaty obligations.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The effective nationality principle, drawn from the ICJ's Nottebohm judgment, determines which of two competing citizenships is 'genuine' when both states assert claims. Factors include habitual residence, family connections, and economic activity.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: India has not ratified the 1961 UN Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness. India is not legally bound by its obligations. However, India's domestic provisions (Section 3 birth citizenship, Section 6 naturalization exceptions) address statelessness as a policy matter.
• Statement 3 — Correct: If a naturalization applicant's original country legally prohibits formal renunciation, the Indian government may waive the renunciation requirement and proceed with naturalization — preventing the person from becoming stateless as a consequence of the Indian requirement.

Value Addition:
• India has also not ratified the 1951 Refugee Convention — its refugee policy is entirely discretionary and administrative.
• The Nottebohm case (Liechtenstein v. Guatemala, 1955) is the foundational ICJ precedent on effective nationality.
• Statelessness creates a legal limbo where a person loses all state protection — a significant human rights concern addressed in international law but not uniformly in domestic law.
